output.title: Why proof-of-concept debt survives
output.body:
Proof-of-concept debt usually survives for one boring reason: the pilot solved part of the problem, but nobody made it part of daily work. A small business can run the manual version for weeks, build a clever demo, and still keep the old process because the last mile is where the real cost sits: who owns it, who watches it, and who fixes it when it breaks.

I’d treat that as a bounded workflow decision, not a vague “use AI more” question. Pick one recurring workflow — customer questions, invoice entry, lead routing, or data sync — and ask whether it is frequent, repeatable, and measurable. If it is, the next question is simple: once the automation works, who owns running it day to day?

That matters because automation without operational ownership turns into shelf-ware. And shelf-ware is just debt with a cleaner label.

Bareni’s diagnostic is built around that check. It starts with one recurring workflow, says honestly whether AI fits, and if it does, defines pilot scope, fixed price, and measures. Finished code is handed to the customer, and the accounts stay in the customer’s name from the start. Timings are intended scopes, not guarantees.

If you cannot name the owner of the workflow, the problem is not the model. It is the operating decision. Clarify that first, before you build another pilot.
